description.narrative:
Impact: Afghan women and girls have their human rights protected and promoted through access to essential services, humanitarian assistance, livelihoods and income opportunities, improved voice and agency and support from a resilient Afghan women's movement.
OUTCOME 1.1 By the end of 2025, more people in Afghanistan, particularly the most marginalized, will be able to equitably access essential services that meet minimum quality standards.
OUTCOME 1.2 By the end of 2025, more people in Afghanistan, notably women and vulnerable groups, will benefit from an increasingly inclusive economy, with greater equality of economic opportunities, jobs, more resilient livelihoods, strengthened food value chains, and improved natural resources management.
OUTCOME 1.3 By the end of 2025, more people in Afghanistan can participate in an increasingly socially cohesive, gender equal, and inclusive society, where the rule of law and human rights are progressively upheld, and more people can participate in governance and decision-making.
Outcome 1.4: By end of 2025, the UN system in Afghanistan, Member States and regional organizations effectively contribute to progress on gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls in Afghanistan.

Insatsen fokuserar på att skydda och främja afghanska kvinnor och flickors mänskliga rättigheter genom tillgång till nödvändig service, humanitärt bistånd, försörjning och inkomstmöjligheter, möjligheter att delta och göra sina röster hörda samt en motståndskraftig afghansk kvinnorörelse.

The contribution is aiming to protect and promote Afghan women and girls human rights through access to essential services, humanitarian assistance, livelihoods and income opportunities, improved voice and agency and support from a resilient Afghan women's movement.

sector.narrative: Women’s rights organisations and movements, and government institutions

description.narrative:
In 2024, UN Women reached more than 229,000 women and girls in Afghanistan with lifesaving and basic services, while thousands of women strengthened their livelihoods through vocational training, business support, and savings groups. UN Women also continued to amplify womens voices in international processes through national consultations in all provinces and provided support to more than 240 womenled civil society organizations.
At the same time, the year was marked by several unexpected and negative developments, primarily linked to the introduction of the PVPV Law, which severely restricted womens mobility, access to the justice system, and public services. The PVPV Law is a morality law that codifies and intensifies the existing restrictions enforced by the de facto authorities by sharply limiting womens mobility, visibility, and agencyincluding requirements for full coverage, mandatory male accompaniment in public spaces, silence in public settings, and extensive powers for the state to monitor and punish.
These developments led to increased protection needs nationwide, deteriorating mental health, and further marginalization of women in the labour market. The economic situation worsened beyond previous forecasts, and women owned businesses proved more vulnerable than those owned by men. The year also brought some unexpected positive effects, such as local authorities in certain provinces beginning to request womens participation in community interventions after observing concrete results, and UN Women successfully negotiating the reopening of public spaces for women, including the Bande Amir area.
UN Women also succeeded, through evidence based advocacy, in having several restrictive measures modified or withdrawn, such as the requirement for womens organizations to change their names. Taken together, the results highlight both the continued importance of UN Womens work in an extremely restrictive environment and the growing gap between womens rights and prevailing political realities.
